Local media needs support if devolution push is to succeed, publishers say
article.full_text: Greater support for local media is needed to hold mayors and councils to account under Andy Burnham’s plans for devolution, which would involve a massive transfer of power into local government, publishers have said. A range of figures involved with local news broadly welcomed new plans unveiled by the prime minister, but said that monetising content, barriers erected by populist politicians and the roles of big tech and the BBC were among the challenges they faced. Theo Bamber, the chief executive of the News Media Association, the trade body representing UK national, regional and local news publishers, said that any moves to give people greater control would be an illusion unless the decisions affecting their lives could be scrutinised by trusted and professional local journalists. “We were interested that the government’s announcements about greater devolution have not mentioned press or media policy,” he said. “We believe that is a mistake because the two should not be siloed and, ultimately, the success of devolution is dependent on scrutiny.” Bamber said that 46 million people a month were consuming local media and that this was proof of the resilience of the sector. He also said it was a counter to the proliferation of misinformation amid unrest in Southampton and Belfast recently. However, as No 10 moved to devolve more power from Westminster to regions, there was also concern that these plans came as some journalists found their access to meetings was being limited, or were being sidelined as policymakers cut down on press conferences or chose to use social media instead. A Reform UK council leader’s decision to ban his councillors from engaging with a prominent local newspaper was condemned last year as a “massive attack on local democracy” and a sign of things to come should the party form the next government. There has also been unease that Keir Starmer’s administration appeared to embrace influencers, and that Burnham has been relatively slow to make himself available to face questions. The National Union of Journalists (NUJ) warned that a lack of a strong local news sector would threaten any devolution agenda and that support could not be left to the “vagaries of the market”. “Access to trusted local news is essential for democracy to thrive. However, millions across the UK now live in news deserts and the industry has faced decades of decline,” said Laura Davison, the NUJ general secretary, who noted large-scale job losses and the fact that about 300 local papers had closed since 2005.” John McDonnell, the veteran Labour MP and secretary of the NUJ’s parliamentary group, said: “If power is to be devolved on any scale then there is an even greater need for securing the role of local media to report on and hold local decision makers to account. This needs resourcing to make effective.” Under a scheme announced earlier this year, the government will provide up to £12m of funding over two years to support local news outlets as it tries to fill so-called “news deserts”. Local media outlets in print, online, radio or TV can bid for grants to support their financial sustainability and transition to digital business models under the new fund. However, there are calls for additional support, including from those involved in startups seeking to make up for the lack of an established news outlet in some areas. Mike Harris, the publisher of the Lead, an independent progressive digital newspaper, said: “We’ve launched the first new local titles in many of the communities in the UK most at threat from the far right, but it’s unbelievably challenging making the business model work. “People in working-class communities do donate and subscribe to our local newspapers but it’s hard to make the model work in comparison with launching in wealthier cities with lots of middle-class professionals.
